summary: Describes the transport mechanisms for carrying Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) messages: HTTP, file, mail, and TCP. CMC defines the messages for certificate requests and responses, and this document covers how to move them between clients and certificate authorities. It was replaced by RFC 10003.

plainLanguage.summary: A certificate request is a letter asking a certificate authority to issue a certificate. This RFC lists the ways to deliver that letter and the answer, and says how each way should label the envelope so the receiver knows what is inside.

questions: how to send cmc messages over http
which port does cmc over tcp use
subtitle: Four ways to move CMC certificate request and response messages: files, mail, HTTP and plain TCP.

tldr.problem: CMC defines the messages for requesting and issuing certificates, but clients and certificate authorities still need agreed ways to carry those messages between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four transports: files with fixed extensions, MIME mail, HTTP POST with set content types, and raw TCP with no wrapping.
tldr.outcome: Different environments, from off-line clients to web servers, can exchange CMC messages in an interoperable way. RFC 10003 has replaced this document.

today: RFC 5273 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 10003 and updated by RFC 6402, so use those for the current CMC transport rules.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
This document defines transport methods for moving CMC messages, which are defined in RFC 5272. The transport mechanisms described here are HTTP, file, mail and TCP.

CMC messages come as Simple PKI Requests and Responses, and as Full PKI Requests and Responses. The transports differ mostly in how they label and wrap those four message types. The document uses the usual RFC 2119 key words such as MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY and REQUIRED, which say how strictly a requirement applies.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate request is a letter. This document lists the ways to deliver the letter, and the answer to it, and how to write on the envelope so the receiver knows what is inside.

sections.title: File-Based Protocol
sections.content:
Enrollment messages and responses may be transferred between clients and servers using file-system mechanisms, such as when enrollment is performed for an off-line client, meaning a client that is not connected to the network at the time. When files are used to transport binary Full PKI Request or Full PKI Response messages, there MUST be only one instance of a request or response message in a single file.

The RFC gives the file type extensions that SHOULD be used. A Simple PKI Request uses the extension .p10, a Full PKI Request uses .crq, a Simple PKI Response uses .p7c and a Full PKI Response uses .crp.
sections.plainLanguage: One message goes in one file, and the file name ends with a short code that says which of the four message types it holds.

sections.title: Mail-Based Protocol
sections.content:
MIME wrapping is defined for those environments that are MIME native, and the basic MIME wrapping here is taken from the S/MIME Version 3.1 Message Specification. When using a mail-based protocol, MIME wrapping between the layers of CMS wrapping is optional, which differs from a standard S/MIME message.

Simple enrollment requests are encoded using the application/pkcs10 content type. A file name MUST be included either in a content-type or a content-disposition statement, and the extension for the file MUST be .p10. Simple enrollment response messages MUST be encoded as content type application/pkcs7-mime, with an smime-type parameter of certs-only and a .p7c file name. Full enrollment request messages use the same content type with an smime-type value of CMC-Request and a .p7m file name, and full enrollment response messages use CMC-response with a .p7m file name.
sections.plainLanguage: In email, the attachment carries a label that says which kind of message it is and a file name whose ending matches that label.

sections.title: HTTP-Based Protocol
sections.content:
In most circumstances, the use of HTTP over TLS provides the content protection needed against eavesdroppers. For CMC clients and servers using HTTP to interoperate, the rules are fixed. Clients MUST use the POST method to submit their requests. Servers MUST use the 200 response code for successful responses. Clients MAY attempt to send HTTP requests using TLS 1.0 or later, although servers are not required to support TLS. Servers MUST NOT assume client support for any type of HTTP authentication such as cookies, Basic authentication, or Digest authentication.

A PKI Request sent with the POST method carries a Content-Type header with the appropriate value from the MIME table, and a body that is the binary value of the encoding of the PKI Request. An HTTP-based PKI Response is composed of the appropriate HTTP headers followed by the binary value of the BER (Basic Encoding Rules) encoding of either a Simple or Full PKI Response, and its Content-Type header MUST have the appropriate value from the same table.
sections.plainLanguage: Over the web, the client posts the request and the server answers with a success code and the encoded reply. The two sides agree on the content type from the same table the mail transport uses.

sections.title: TCP-Based Protocol
sections.content:
When CMC messages are sent over a TCP-based connection, no wrapping is required. Messages are sent in their binary encoded form. The client closes a connection after receiving a response, or it issues another request to the server using the same connection. Reusing one connection for multiple successive requests, instead of opening multiple connections that are only used for a single request, is RECOMMENDED for performance and resource conservation reasons. A server MAY close a connection after it has been idle for some period of time, and this timeout would typically be several minutes long.

There is no specific port to be used for TCP-based transport. Only the Private Ports 49152-65535 may be used in this manner without registration, and the ports in the range of 1-49151 SHOULD NOT be used. The port to be used is configured out of band, which means both ends agree on it beforehand instead of carrying it in the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: With plain TCP the bytes go down the connection as they are, with no wrapper. Both ends agree on the port number beforehand, and it should be one from the private range that needs no registration.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms for thwarting replay attacks may be required in particular implementations, depending on the operational environment. In cases where the Certification Authority (CA) maintains significant state information, replay attacks may be detectable without the inclusion of the optional nonce mechanisms. Implementers need to consider the environmental conditions before choosing whether to implement the senderNonce and recipientNonce attributes, and developers of state-constrained PKI clients are strongly encouraged to incorporate the use of these attributes.

Setting up a secure channel between an end-entity and a CA or Registration Authority (RA), and likewise between an RA and another RA or CA, requires an out-of-band trust initiation mechanism, for example IPsec or TLS. Many such schemes exist and the choice of any particular scheme is outside the scope of the document. In some instances no prior out-of-band trust will have been initiated, which can occur when the protocol itself is used to download onto the system the set of trust anchors. In these instances the Enveloped Data content type must be used, to give the same protection that TLS would have provided.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could copy an old message and send it again, so some systems add one-time numbers that make an old message useless. The two ends also need a way to trust each other before the exchange starts, because the transports themselves do not provide it.

items.title: File
items.text: One message per file, with a fixed extension per message type.

items.title: Mail
items.text: MIME wrapping, with a content type and an smime-type value.

items.title: HTTP
items.text: POST from the client, 200 from the server, body in binary form.

items.title: TCP
items.text: No wrapping at all; the message is sent in its binary encoded form.
